lifeStatusScope.wild: Free-ranging field ecology was not assessed. The genetic studies summarized here did not sample a known wild population of Hylobates agilis.
lifeStatusScope.domesticated: Domestication was not assessed. One study used captive zoo samples and gibbons reared by local residents; those samples are not treated as wild population evidence.
lifeStatusScope.fossil: Fossil occurrence and geological age were not assessed.

gaps: No morphology evidence was assessed in this batch.
Reproduction, development, lifespan and other life-history traits have not been assessed.
The genetic sample studies do not assess habitat use, diet, behavior or ecological interactions.

claims.text: In a Y-chromosome analysis of 26 captive male gibbons from 10 species, including three H. agilis, the concatenated seven-amplicon tree left H. agilis, H. moloch and H. klossii in an unresolved trichotomy. The authors report weakly supported nodes and insufficient sampled Y-chromosome variation to resolve relationships among these rapidly diverged Hylobates species; this is a limited paternal-lineage result, not a complete species tree.
claims.locator: Methods, Gibbon DNA samples and PCR amplification of Y chromosome loci; Results, Phylogenetic analyses; Discussion, Y chromosome and mtDNA phylogenies of Hylobates species
claims.placeTimeScope: Long-term author sample collections; the 26 male samples were originally collected during routine veterinary examinations of captive gibbons. H. agilis sample n=3. The paper does not report collection dates or known geographic provenance for these H. agilis individuals; article published in 2012.
claims.lifeStatus: Captive male samples; no free-ranging H. agilis are included in this Y-chromosome sample.

claims.text: A second study collected blood from 37 H. agilis individuals at zoos in Indonesia and Thailand and from gibbons reared by local residents in Kalimantan; two H. agilis samples were excluded from opsin genotyping. Across 152 genotyped gibbons from eight species, the study found standard L and M opsin genes and no L/M hybrid genes. In male samples from five species, including H. agilis, the authors detected L/M opsin gene-conversion tracts predominantly in introns. These are sample-bounded genetic findings; the study did not measure individual color-vision behavior or establish species-wide prevalence.
claims.locator: Methods, Gibbon DNA samples; Results, L/M opsin genotyping; Results, Test of gene conversion by GENECONV; Figure 4 legend
claims.placeTimeScope: Blood samples came from Ragunan and Pontianak zoos in Indonesia, Chiang Mai, Bangkok and Khao Kheow Open zoos in Thailand, and locally reared gibbons in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Sampling dates are not stated in the cited Methods; article published in 2011. Two of the 37 H. agilis samples were not opsin-genotyped.
claims.lifeStatus: Zoo-held and locally reared samples; the article does not identify these as free-ranging wild animals. The findings describe assayed genotypes, not measured visual behavior.

gaps: Evidence is limited to captive or locally reared samples, a small H. agilis Y-chromosome sample and marker-specific genetic analyses; it does not establish a comprehensive species phylogeny, wild-population variation or organism-level visual phenotype.
Sample collection locations do not form a range inventory or establish wild occurrence localities.
No fossil evidence or geological age was assessed.
No threat status, population trend or range-wide conservation assessment was assessed.

reasons: Only two bounded genetics studies were assessed; six facets remain not-assessed.
Evidence is sample-limited and does not provide wild population, range-wide or species-wide coverage.
No independent expert review has been completed.
